content: The follow-up patients who achieved treatment success (SVR12) were calculated by adding the number of participants who reached SVR12 to those lost to follow-up, and dividing this sum by the total number of participants who completed treatment. In this analysis, participants lost to follow-up were considered as having achieved SVR12 in the numerator and were included in the denominator. Patients still undergoing treatment or follow-up were excluded from the efficacy analyses. In the intention-to-treat (ITT), modified ITT, and sensitivity analysis 1, patients lost to follow-up were classified as non-responders (i.e., they did not achieve SVR12). Sensitivity analysis 2 assumed a best-case scenario, where those lost to follow-up were considered to have achieved SVR12. Patients who discontinued treatment were excluded from the per-protocol (PP) analysis and both sensitivity analyses, but they were included in the ITT and modified ITT analyses based on their reported SVR12 outcomes. For safety assessments, we considered serious adverse events, as well as common side effects such as headache, fatigue or asthenia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, cough, and other frequently reported events. The proportion of participants experiencing adverse events was calculated based on the number of participants who received at least one dose of treatment (modified ITT analysis). The discontinuation rate was determined by dividing the number of participants who discontinued treatment by the total number of participants who received at least one dose of treatment. We documented the duration of treatment, the time of discontinuation, and the reasons for discontinuation (including adverse events), when available. Studies reporting quality-of-life outcomes were narratively summarized. Few studies considered quality of life as an outcome, and the measures used were heterogeneous. For statistical analysis, pooled proportions were calculated using the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation. Random-effects models were applied to all analyses. The primary analysis included pooled studies regardless of patient age, cirrhosis status, treatment duration, treatment type (approved or unapproved regimens for children), genotype, prior treatment history (including direct-acting antiviral [DAA] or interferon-based regimens), or study design (observational versus clinical studies). Subgroup analyses were conducted based on age (3–5 years, 6–11 years, and 12–18 years) and, for SVR12, according to the aforementioned variables. Stratified analyses by HIV status or other medical conditions were not performed due to insufficient data. Results of stratified analyses by treatment duration could be confounded by patient factors (e.g., cirrhosis, prior treatment, genotype) that influenced treatment duration. Statistical heterogeneity between studies and groups was assessed using Cochran’s Q test, and the I² statistic was reported to quantify heterogeneity. Heterogeneity was considered unimportant for I² values below 40%, moderate for values between 30% and 60%, substantial for values between 50% and 90%, and considerable for values above 75%. To evaluate the certainty of evidence, the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach was used, adapted for the unique clinical and methodological characteristics of DAA regimen research. In the traditional GRADE framework, randomized trials start as high-quality evidence, while non-randomized studies start as low-quality evidence due to their susceptibility to bias and confounding. However, for DAA regimens, several factors increased the certainty of findings from non-randomized studies: (1) SVR12 is an objective outcome measure, (2) spontaneous SVR rates are extremely low, (3) SVR rates with DAA regimens are very high, and (4) SVR rates are consistent between randomized and non-randomized studies. To reflect this higher certainty, non-randomized studies were graded as moderate-certainty evidence. Certainty could be downgraded for risk of bias (if >30% of patients were from studies with serious or unknown risk of bias), inconsistency (if I² >40%), imprecision (if the confidence interval for SVR proportions exceeded 10% or total sample size was <50), indirectness (e.g., differences in populations or interventions), or suspected publication bias (e.g., unpublished studies or studies not reporting SVR12). Certainty could be upgraded for very large effect sizes (pooled SVR ≥96%). Adverse events, being more subjective and difficult to interpret without a comparison group, were assessed as very low-certainty evidence due to high uncertainty. For study selection, 1181 records were identified from PubMed, 107 from Embase, and 21 from conference abstracts. A total of 49 unique studies were included, comprising 34 full-length papers and 15 abstracts. Three studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), 28 were non-randomized controlled trials, and 18 were observational studies. Most studies were conducted in Egypt (24), followed by India (5), Pakistan (2), and other countries. Information on comorbidities was reported in 22 of 49 studies (45%). Some studies included specific pediatric populations, such as those with hematological disorders or cancer survivors. Nine studies included cirrhotic patients, but individual outcomes were not reported. The quality of the included studies was assessed. Most studies had a low risk of bias in intervention classification, outcome measurement, and selection of reported results. Some studies had moderate or high risk of bias due to deviations from intended interventions or missing data.
